newsitem.title: JAPAN: Failure of Japan insurer shows lingering headache.
newsitem.headline: Failure of Japan insurer shows lingering headache.

text.p: Japan appears to be moving more aggressively to clean up its long-running bad-loan mess, but the failure of a medium-sized life insurer is a reminder -- if any were needed -- that big headaches still remain.

The Finance Ministry said on Friday it had ordered Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co to halt all operations except for servicing current customers, the first time the government has forced an insurer to shut down in the postwar period.
The move, which will result in the insurer's liquidation, was the latest in a series of financial failures since 1995, when Japan suffered its first bank failure since World War Two.

Earlier this month, Nippon Credit Bank Ltd, one of the nation's wobbliest banks, unveiled a sweeping restructuring plan, including a pullout from overseas business. That same day, troubled Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd announced a plan to merge with regional rival, Hokkaido Bank Ltd.

"If you ask me right now, it looks very good that the authorities know what they are doing and the consolidation is being managed effectively and more speedily than over the last five years," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan.

Japanese financial institutions have struggled for seven years to shake off the bad-loan hangover left from the collapse of the 1980s "bubble economy" of sky-high asset prices. Many construction and property firms have similar woes.

"It (the shutdown order) is a sign of a bit more action (by authorities), but at this stage, it's merely pointing to the breadth of the problem," said David Threadgold, financial analyst at BZW Securities. "It's not just a banking problem," he said. "It's pretty widely spread."

Many life insurers suffer from the same bad-loan woes that afflict the financial system generally, but they have also been hit by the hyper-easy credit policy kept in place for nearly two years to help out banks and keep the nation's economic recovery on track, analysts said.

Low interest rates have eroded yields on insurers' investments, forcing some into risky business in an attempt to boost profits to cover losses on non-performing loans, they said. "They (insurers) are a victim of the low-interest policy," said Yukiko Ohara, an analyst at UBS Securities Ltd.

News of Nissan Life's failure sparked a vague market rumour that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) may raise interest rates next month, but BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita squelched the talk when he told a parliamentary panel the central bank would not tighten credit until it had confirmed Japan's economic recovery.
Other insurance companies face tough times ahead of Japan's planned "Big Bang" financial deregulation, which aims to break down barriers among brokers, banks and insurers by 2001.

Ratings agency Moody's Investors Service Inc said in January that insurers' competitiveness was declining due to their large portfolios of low-yielding stocks, inefficient distribution and high and rigid cost structures.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said no other life insurers were in the same straits as Nissan Life, but added that the ministry would deal swiftly with any future failures.
He also pledged to protect Nissan Life's policyholders and said the Life Insurance Association of Japan was being asked to manage the insurer's business and assets.
A ministry official said the government was not considering the use of public funds in the wind-up scheme and was discussing a safety net to protect policyholders.

Domestic media said the Life Insurance Industry Association would draw up details of the Nissan Life wind-up scheme, including the use of money contributed by other life insurers to a fund to help transfer policies to healthy firms.

Analysts, however, questioned just how long authorities could stick to their current stance, which rules out using tax money to clean up the broader bad-loan mess and relies on stronger firms to share the burden when weaker rivals fail.
Public outrage flared last year over the budgeting of 685 billion yen ($5.43 billion) to help liquidate failed "jusen" mortgage firms.

"There will be a lot of problems emerging in the run-up to the 'Big Bang' and it will take a lot of money to resolve them," Ohara said. "The government is emphasising fiscal reform (to cut the budget deficit) and so is turning to the healthier banks and life insurers. But they can't keep doing that -- eventually the government will have to pay." ($1=126 yen)
